amendments.why: PRO.26.15 renders nil'ah, a 3ms finite verb, as 'It wearieth him to bring it again to his mouth': the ASV recasts the clause impersonally and demotes the verb's own subject to the English object. Rule 44's supplied-object paragraph, read literally, excludes that pronoun twice over — it is an object, and it is one 'the Hebrew does not write' — so it would be marked added and the verb's only subject would go unrendered against rule 2, while the anticipatory It would have no home either. The rule's examples are all pronouns denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote (the it of vayyappel, the them of vayyashq), which is a different thing from the verb's own person and number written in the case an English recasting forces. The amendment drops the parenthetical 'which is a subject' from the sentence that caused the contradiction and adds a guarded carve-out beside the existing reflexive one, keyed to whom the English pronoun denotes and tested by the same subtraction the rule already uses; it leaves rule 20's ruling on a cleft or impersonal it in a verbless clause untouched, since there no verb stands to be recast. Nothing else in the rule is altered.
amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **But run that same subtraction on the particle before folding it in.** Where the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme and the particle adds a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write, no morpheme licenses that word: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30 and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering, exactly as this rule leaves a supplied object noun `added` and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* keeps its *again* with the verb, discontinuous under rule 25, because *turn* alone does not write the returning, and `כָּנַס` → *gather ... together* and `מָצָא` → *find out* keep theirs on the same ground; but `בּוֹא` hiphil → *bring him* ***back*** leaves the *back* `added`, because the hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **And a pronoun realizing the source verb's own person and number is not a supplied object either, whatever case the English recasting puts it in.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb impersonally — writing a dummy or anticipatory *it* as the English subject and demoting the verb's own subject to the English object — both words belong to that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, exactly as rule 17 keeps a presentative dummy with the finite verb it recasts and rule 21 keeps *it was* with `הָיָה`: `נִלְאָה לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ אֶל־פִּיו` → ***It wearieth him*** *to bring it again to his mouth* gives *It wearieth him* to `נִלְאָה`, while the infinitive and the preposition keep their own English. What the preceding sentences govern is a pronoun denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as the *it* of `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and the *them* of `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* are; a pronoun denoting the very participant the verb's own person and number denote is not that, and marking it `added` would leave the verb's subject unrendered against rule 2 while an English word plainly realizing it stood unaligned. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English pronoun and ask whether a participant the Hebrew wrote has lost its rendering, or only one the ASV supplied. Read whom the pronoun denotes rather than the case English puts it in, and read the Hebrew clause before reaching for this sentence: where an object morpheme stands in the clause it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, where the ASV writes the verb's subject as an English subject this sentence does not arise, and rule 20's ruling that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added` governs a verbless clause, where no verb stands to be recast. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. Where it does carry the lexeme, the noun is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.

conventions: Proverbs' juxtaposed similes were counted rather than assumed. Where a comparative kaph, a correlative ken or a waw stands, it takes the As, like or So the ASV wrote for it (26.1, 26.2, 26.7, 26.8, 26.9, 26.10, 26.11, 26.14, 26.18, 26.21, 26.22); where the Hebrew juxtaposes the two cola with no such morpheme, the word is its own added unit and is not folded into the noun, the participle or the preposition standing beside it (As at 26.9, 26.10, 26.14, 26.21; like at 26.17, 26.23; So at 26.11). One verse may need both readings, as 26.9, 26.10, 26.14 and 26.21 do, where the supplied As opens the verse and a written waw carries the answering So. The genre is not evidence that a particle is present, and the ASV's italics corroborate without deciding (rule 7).

be-eynaw rendered 'in his own conceit' is split three ways and not fused: be- takes in, ayin takes conceit, and the suffix takes the whole emphatic possessive his own under rule 18. Each morpheme holds an English word of its own, so rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet and rule 2 governs, unlike the fused idioms of rules 30 and 40 where the preposition and its noun share a single word. Read identically at 26.5, 26.12 and 26.16, and the marginal literal 'Hebrew his own eyes' was read and set aside under rule 38 in all three. Where no suffix stands, a supplied possessive is added as usual (his own at 26.6, his at 26.26).

In a construct chain the ASV renders attributively (rule 28), each noun takes the English word carrying its own lexeme, whichever of the two stands first in the English: leshon sheqer gives tongue to the construct and lying to the rectum (26.28), ish midyanim gives man and contentious (26.21), kesef sigim gives silver to the construct and dross to the rectum (26.23), and hadre vaten gives parts to heder and innermost to beten (26.22). Position in the English phrase decides nothing; 26.22 is the one place where the division was materially open, and the competing reading is named in that unit's note.

Where it does carry the lexeme, the noun is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amended.why: PRO.26.15 renders nil'ah, a 3ms finite verb, as 'It wearieth him to bring it again to his mouth': the ASV recasts the clause impersonally and demotes the verb's own subject to the English object. Rule 44's supplied-object paragraph, read literally, excludes that pronoun twice over — it is an object, and it is one 'the Hebrew does not write' — so it would be marked added and the verb's only subject would go unrendered against rule 2, while the anticipatory It would have no home either. The rule's examples are all pronouns denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote (the it of vayyappel, the them of vayyashq), which is a different thing from the verb's own person and number written in the case an English recasting forces. The amendment drops the parenthetical 'which is a subject' from the sentence that caused the contradiction and adds a guarded carve-out beside the existing reflexive one, keyed to whom the English pronoun denotes and tested by the same subtraction the rule already uses; it leaves rule 20's ruling on a cleft or impersonal it in a verbless clause untouched, since there no verb stands to be recast. Nothing else in the rule is altered.

report: Checked all 25 candidate lemma groups and read the full dump end to end for the added-versus-folded splits the lemma table cannot see. No cross-verse split found: every difference is licensed by what the ASV wrote or by what stands in the source.

The supplied simile frame is the chapter's largest recurring judgment and is consistent. As/like/So is aligned wherever a morpheme stands for it (the comparative kaph at 26.1, 26.2, 26.8, 26.11, 26.18, 26.22; ken at 26.1, 26.2, 26.8; a waw rendered So at 26.7, 26.9, 26.10, 26.14, 26.21) and added where the Hebrew juxtaposes with none (As at 26.9, 26.10, 26.14, 26.21; like at 26.17, 26.23; So at 26.11, whose second colon writes neither waw nor ken).

Copula placement is uniform against rules 20 and 49: a prepositional predicate carries it on the preposition (26.7, 26.9, 26.12, 26.13, 26.21 twice, 26.22, 26.25), a nominal or adjectival predicate on the predicate word (26.1, 26.8, 26.10, 26.11, 26.16, 26.19, 26.23). The adjunct prepositional phrase at 26.16 is correctly excluded, which is rule 49's closing limit.

Supplied relatives divide on the Hebrew rather than on the English: an articleless attributive participle keeps the relative (26.2, 26.10, 26.11 twice, 26.16), while a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent leaves it added (26.9, 26.19). Substantival participles take He that / he that / one that / Whoso / them that under rule 46 (26.6, 26.8, 26.10, 26.17, 26.24, 26.27), headed on the lexeme each time.

The three 'in his own conceit' verses (26.5, 26.12, 26.16) are split identically three ways rather than fused; the four supplied-the sluggard verses (26.13-26.16), the phrasal particles (26.6, 26.7, 26.9, 26.15, 26.20, 26.22, 26.24) and the attributively rendered construct chains (26.21, 26.22, 26.23, 26.28) each agree with themselves. 26.14's 'So doth' is rule 34's pro-verb, correctly given to the one written tissov.

BSB: none of the four disagreements is a genuine error. Three are rule 40 recastings where the ASV writes a bare object or inverts the clause (be- at 26.11 'repeateth his folly', be- at 26.25 'believe him not', al at 26.23, where the ASV makes cheres the predicate nominal and the supplied 'with' reaches the participle's own complement). The fourth, the suffix on qol at 26.25, is unrendered under either the fused or the split reading of 'he speaketh fair', so it does not turn on that unit's hedged choice. No accepted edge was changed.

One correction, in PRO.26.1 only: the review note said three assimilated article tokens are unrepresented where the verse has four (s002, s005, s009, s012), all unrepresented. The patch returns the alignment verbatim and corrects the note; no edge, head or status changes anywhere in the chapter.

Contract: PRO.26.15 met a case rule 44 had not considered. In 'It wearieth him', the ASV recasts nil'ah impersonally and demotes the verb's own 3ms subject to the English object, so rule 44's supplied-object clause read literally ('which is a subject, and never an object the Hebrew does not write') would mark that pronoun added and leave the verb's subject unrendered. Returned as an amendment narrowing that clause, not as a new rule.
